name: session-facade
intent: Provide a coarse-grained server-side entry point that fronts a set of fine-grained business objects and services, so that one client conversation maps to one workflow-level operation whose transaction, authorization and error handling the facade owns.
problem: A use case is fulfilled by several fine-grained services, business objects and repositories, and every caller that wants that use case has to know the collaboration's shape: which services to invoke, in what order, under which transaction boundary, and how to translate domain failures into client-meaningful errors. Leaving that knowledge in each presentation, batch or remote client couples those tiers to the business tier's internal decomposition, duplicates the orchestration, and turns one conversation into a burst of fine-grained calls.
context: Server-side applications whose business tier is decomposed into many small services, business objects and repositories, and whose clients are use-case-shaped: web controllers, message handlers, batch jobs or remote clients. It applies when the runtime can demarcate a transaction around a method (a Jakarta EE container, Spring @Transactional, .NET scoped services, an ORM session) and when several clients share the same workflows. The facade is stateless by default; a stateful, conversation-scoped facade is the variant for multi-step interactions such as wizards or checkout flows.
benefits: One coarse-grained operation per use case: clients name the conversation ('placeOrder') instead of reproducing the sequence of fine-grained calls, so the orchestration is written once.

Transaction, authorization and error-translation policy is attached at a single boundary instead of being re-implemented per client - the catalog's own formulation is that the facade centralizes transaction control and security management.
Information hiding: business objects, repositories and their interactions become internal to the business tier and can be refactored behind the coarse contract without touching clients.

Fewer boundary crossings: a conversation that would otherwise take several fine-grained calls becomes one, which raises throughput on high-latency boundaries (the pattern's original motivation) and removes repeated per-call overhead locally.
Reuse across channels: the same facade serves web, batch, messaging and remote clients, and a workflow can be exercised in a test without going through the presentation tier.
A natural home for cross-cutting workflow concerns: input validation, idempotency checks, consistency rules spanning several services, and mapping of domain exceptions to stable application errors.
tradeoffs: Facade bloat: without discipline the component absorbs business rules that belong to the domain and becomes a god object. Core J2EE Patterns had to add the Application Service pattern because common logic placed in session facades 'often results in the duplication of code'.
Pass-through risk: a facade with one method per fine-grained call adds a layer without raising granularity, so clients stay chatty and the indirection buys nothing (the Middle Man smell).
Mapping cost: a coarse boundary wants its own request and response shapes, so Transfer-Object-to-domain mapping and its boilerplate appear where direct calls needed none.
Interface gravity: the facade contract is what clients compile against, so coarse methods evolve more slowly than the domain behind them, and a signature change ripples to every client.
Transaction scope: making the facade method the unit of work easily produces long transactions when the workflow waits on remote calls or slow I/O, holding locks and exhausting connection pools.

Extra dependency in the call path, and a scaling liability when the facade is stateful: conversation-scoped instances must be expired and cleaned up, while pooled stateless instances must not keep per-request state.

participants.responsibility: Presentation, batch or remote caller that invokes one coarse operation per conversation and never reaches the business tier's fine-grained components directly.

The coarse-grained boundary: one operation per use case that sequences the participants, owns the transaction boundary and the authorization hand-off, translates domain failures into stable application errors, and keeps business rules out of itself.
Fine-grained domain component that performs the actual work of the use case (pricing, inventory, order creation) and knows nothing about the facade's clients.
Optional role added to the catalog's second edition: holds logic shared by several facades so it is not duplicated among them.
Persistence gateway used directly by the facade in applications that have no business objects and only trivial logic to encapsulate.
Coarse request/response payload that crosses the facade boundary in one hop instead of exposing entities or forcing chatty accessors.

use_cases: Web or API controllers that must fulfil a use case spanning several services (pricing, inventory, payment, notification) in one transactional call instead of a controller-level call sequence.

Remote or rich clients that would otherwise make chatty fine-grained calls; the facade is exposed as the remote business interface, usually together with a client-side Business Delegate and Transfer Objects.
Batch jobs, schedulers and message consumers that reuse the same workflow entry points as the interactive tier rather than duplicating the orchestration.
Multi-channel applications (web, mobile, admin console) that need one business-tier API with identical authorization, validation and transaction semantics.
Multi-step conversations such as checkout or onboarding wizards, where a stateful, conversation-scoped facade holds the intermediate state instead of the client juggling it.
Modernization of a tangled fine-grained service tier: a coarse facade in front of the existing services lets clients migrate to a clean use-case API incrementally.

Oracle ADF Business Components ships this boundary as a framework feature: an Application Module per coarse-grained end-user task exposes service methods on a client interface for UI binding and a service interface for integration, is taken from a pool for a logical unit of work that can span multiple pages, and coordinates commit/rollback over the entity objects behind its view objects.

The Apache NetBeans 'Session Beans for Entity Classes' wizard generates the pattern mechanically - one @Stateless session facade per JPA entity, each extending an AbstractFacade that owns the EntityManager via @PersistenceContext and is injected with @EJB - which is also the canonical degenerate shape: CRUD facades per entity rather than use-case-shaped operations per conversation.

Oracle WebLogic Server's EJB design guidance prescribes it for boundary performance: use a session facade 'to contain complex interactions and reduce calls from Web applications to RMI objects', letting the facade access entity beans locally, collect the data in a structure and return it by value - together with the matching exception that local entity instances should be accessed directly rather than through a facade.
avoid_when: Single-service CRUD endpoints: calling the application service or repository directly is shorter, and the facade would only forward.

The framework already provides the boundary (a Spring @Service class, a NestJS provider, an ASP.NET Core application service): a second session-facade layer on top duplicates a boundary that already exists.
Only local callers and no cross-cutting concern: with no transaction, authorization or mapping policy to centralize, plain orchestration at the call site (or a single transaction script) is simpler.
The domain already exposes a natural coarse-grained API: when an aggregate root's methods already express the use case, that aggregate is the boundary and a separate facade adds a hop.
Pure message-driven designs: a message handler is already one coarse unit of work with its own transaction and error channel, so an extra facade class rarely earns its keep.
anti_patterns: Chatty facade: one facade method per fine-grained service call, preserving the coupling and the call count the pattern exists to remove.
God facade: business rules, validation and persistence logic accumulate in the facade, so domain logic leaks out of the business objects and the class becomes the hardest in the system to test.
Facade per entity ('CustomerFacade', 'OrderFacade' with CRUD methods): granularity stays entity-shaped and clients still orchestrate the use case themselves.
Stateless facade holding per-client state in instance fields: because the runtime pools or shares instances, that state leaks across requests - a concurrency bug hidden behind a familiar shape.
Leaking entities across the boundary: returning domain objects lets clients navigate the object graph lazily, reintroducing chatty access and tight coupling to the model's internals.
Remote calls or long I/O inside the transaction the facade owns, so the unit of work spans the network and holds locks for its duration.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: protocol and presentation stay outside, domain rules stay inside; the facade only orchestrates and translates.

Information hiding: only the coarse interface is exported; business objects, their interactions and the persistence strategy stay internal (the catalog describes the session facade as playing a Broker role for them).
Stable, coarse-grained boundary contracts: methods are use-case-shaped, so clients depend on a surface that changes far less often than the domain.
Single responsibility and use-case cohesion: one facade per workflow cluster, not per entity or table.
Dependency inversion: the facade depends on the abstractions of the components it coordinates, and clients depend on the facade's contract rather than on those components.
Own your unit of work: the transaction boundary is a deliberate design decision placed at the coarse operation.
Law of Demeter at the boundary: clients interact with one facade, not with the object graph behind it.
best_practices: Design methods as whole conversations ('placeOrder', 'approveInvoice') with coarse request and response payloads (Transfer Objects); never mirror the fine-grained service API.
Orchestrate, do not decide: keep business rules in the business objects or Application Services; the facade sequences calls, validates input, owns the transaction and translates errors.
Keep the facade stateless by default so pooled or shared instances stay safe; use a stateful facade only for genuine multi-step conversations and give it explicit expiry and cleanup.
Bind the transaction to the coarse operation and keep remote calls, file I/O and notifications outside it, registering post-commit work where the platform supports it.
Enforce authorization at the facade entry point - the single place every client passes through - and translate domain exceptions into stable application errors there.
Evolve the coarse contract additively: add new use-case methods instead of changing existing signatures, and version the contract when clients deploy independently.
Extract logic shared by several facades into an Application Service instead of duplicating it, so the facades stay thin and consistent.
sources: Alur, Crupi & Malks, Core J2EE Patterns: Best Practices and Design Strategies, 2nd edition (2003) - 'Session Facade' (Business Tier), including the Stateless and Stateful Session Facade strategies.
